strengths: The paper addresses an important deployment problem: estimating model performance when production labels are unavailable. Combining density-ratio estimation with confidence calibration is a practical approach that avoids retraining the monitored model.

The evaluation is substantial within tabular classification: 603 model–dataset pairs, five Folktables tasks, three classifier families, and 34,953 production chunks, with separate training, reference, and production years.

M-CBPE achieves the lowest aggregate estimation errors across accuracy, AUROC, and F1 in Tables 1–2. For example, F1 RRMSE is 0.19 versus 0.24 for CBPE and 0.25 for IW. Evaluating both numerical estimates and monitoring alerts adds practical value.

The overall pipeline is understandable, public datasets and a code repository are identified, and limitations involving concept shift, support overlap, and effective sample size are explicitly acknowledged. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: The central guarantee is incorrect as stated. Equation (4) establishes calibration conditional on the calibrated score, whereas Equation (3) evaluates decisions based on the original score. Calibration can merge groups with different original decisions. For example, take equally likely scores 0.25 and 0.75 with labels 1 and 0, respectively, and map both scores to 0.5. With identical reference and production distributions, this map is perfectly calibrated, yet Equation (3) estimates accuracy 0.5 while the original classifier, thresholded at 0.5, has accuracy 0. Thus the claimed calibration-error bound fails. Additional conditions, such as estimating E[Y|f(X)] on the target distribution, are needed.

There are material internal inconsistencies. Appendix A swaps the true-negative and false-negative formulas; if implemented literally, this affects F1 and AUROC estimation. It is unclear whether this is only a manuscript error. Also, Section 4.2 specifies a 3-SE alert threshold, but Table 3 reports accuracy-alert F1 of 0.65 for M-CBPE, whereas Figure 3 shows approximately 0.56 at that threshold and reaches 0.65 near 2 SE. The actual threshold-selection protocol needs clarification.

The experimental breadth does not support the universal claims. All tasks use one census-data family and binary classification; temporal changes do not establish that the shifts satisfy the assumed invariant label conditional. Controlled covariate-shift experiments would help isolate the mechanism. Pooled chunk averages also give larger datasets more influence, and no uncertainty estimates or task/model-level breakdowns establish how consistently the gains hold. The chunk-size study covers only one state–task combination.

Important implementation details are missing from the manuscript despite the repository link: the density-ratio classifier and calibrator families, their objectives and hyperparameters, probability calibration, weight stabilization, and validation procedures. Algorithm 1 predicts density ratios on the same reference observations used to train the discriminator, without explaining how overfitting is controlled. These choices directly affect both reproducibility and reliability.

Some baseline comparisons have limited interpretability. ATC is extended to F1 and AUROC without justification, while DoC uses random subsampling to simulate shifts, which need not represent systematic deployment changes. These adaptations do not substantiate broad superiority over the original methods, although the comparisons with IW and CBPE remain useful.

Originality is primarily the combination of existing density-ratio estimation and CBPE through weighted calibration. The theoretical ingredients are attributed to prior work, but the relationship to existing importance-weighted calibration is insufficiently developed, and there is no analysis explaining when the proposed estimator improves on direct IW. The promising empirical contribution does not outweigh the unresolved guarantee and evaluation issues.
